title: Bioengineered Chewing Gum Wiped Out 93% of Cancer-Linked HPV in Patient Samples, Penn Study Finds
excerpt: A plant-based gum made from lablab beans eliminated oral HPV and two bacterial species tied to head and neck cancer without harming beneficial microbes, researchers say.
body:
• Extracts from a bioengineered chewing gum reduced oral HPV levels by 93% in saliva and 80% in oral rinse samples from cancer patients.
  • A single dose of the gum also reduced two bacteria linked to head and neck cancer — P. gingivalis and F. nucleatum — to near-undetectable levels.
  • Unlike radiation therapy, the gum preserved beneficial oral bacteria, offering a more targeted approach to fighting cancer-associated microbes.
  • The study, published in Scientific Reports, could lead to clinical trials for an affordable, non-invasive cancer prevention tool.

A New Weapon Against Oral Cancer

Researchers at the University of Pennsylvania School of Dental Medicine have developed a bioengineered chewing gum that dramatically reduces three microbes associated with head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), one of the most common and aggressive cancers of the mouth and throat.

The study, led by Henry Daniell, the W.D. Miller Professor in Penn Dental Medicine's Department of Basic and Translational Sciences, found that extracts from the gum cut HPV levels by 93% in saliva samples and 80% in oral rinse samples collected from HNSCC patients. The findings were published in Scientific Reports.

"The global increase in oropharyngeal cancer is linked to HPV infection. And Pg and Fn infections worsen survival rates of untreated recurrent or metastatic oral cancer, even after surgery and risk-adjusted adjuvant therapies."

— Henry Daniell, W.D. Miller Professor, Penn Dental Medicine

How the Gum Works

The chewing gum is made from lablab beans and contains a naturally occurring antiviral protein called FRIL. This protein binds to viral glycoproteins on the surface of HPV, trapping the virus and preventing it from entering host cells.

When the team bioengineered the gum to also include protegrin, an antimicrobial peptide capable of killing harmful bacteria, a single dose reduced levels of Porphyromonas gingivalis and Fusobacterium nucleatum — two bacterial species implicated in cancer progression — to near-zero in laboratory samples. Critically, the treatment preserved the beneficial bacteria normally found in the mouth.

That selectivity sets it apart from conventional cancer therapies. Radiation treatment, while effective against tumours, wipes out helpful oral bacteria and promotes the growth of disease-causing yeast such as Candida albicans, according to the study.

Why It Matters

Head and neck squamous cell carcinoma is the seventh most common cancer worldwide among adolescents, young adults, and middle-aged adults, according to Daniell. Despite decades of drug development, most recently approved treatments have not significantly improved five-year survival rates or quality of life for patients, particularly those diagnosed at advanced stages.

The oral microbiome's role in cancer is increasingly well-documented. HPV-16, a high-risk strain, can integrate into the human genome and trigger cancerous changes. Meanwhile, P. gingivalis and F. nucleatum have been linked to worse outcomes in patients with recurrent or metastatic disease, even after surgery and supplemental therapies.

An affordable, plant-based chewing gum that eliminates these threats without the side effects of radiation could represent a meaningful addition to oncologists' toolkit.

What Comes Next

The research remains at the laboratory stage — the gum has not yet been tested in live clinical trials. But Daniell sees a clear path forward.

"Our findings support the value of advancing these therapies to clinical trials as adjuvants with current treatments or as prophylaxis to prevent infection and transmission."

— Henry Daniell, University of Pennsylvania

Co-authors on the study include researchers from Penn Dental Medicine, the University of Kansas Medical Center, UCLA, and the Veterans Administration Greater Los Angeles Healthcare System. The work was funded by the National Institutes of Health, the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and the National Cancer Institute.

If clinical trials confirm the lab results, the gum could eventually serve as a low-cost preventive measure for high-risk populations — a simple, daily habit that might reduce the burden of one of the world's most common cancers.
